::: {#exm-khan-pvalues}
#### Testing every gene in the Khan data

For each of the 2308 genes,
[Welch's two-sample t-test](basic-statistical-methods.qmd#def-two-sample-t-test)
compares mean expression between tumor classes 2 and 4:

```{r}
#| label: khan-pvalues
#| code-fold: false
gene_names <- setdiff(names(khan_pair), "tumor_class")
khan_p <- vapply(
  khan_pair[gene_names],
  function(x) t.test(x ~ khan_pair$tumor_class)$p.value,
  numeric(1)
)
m <- length(khan_p)
c(
  tests = m,
  p_at_most_0.05 = sum(khan_p <= 0.05),
  expected_if_all_null = 0.05 * m
)
```

`r sum(khan_p <= 0.05)` of the `r m` genes have a p-value of at most 0.05.
If every null hypothesis were true,
the p-values would be uniform on $[0, 1]$ and about `r 0.05 * m` genes would fall below 0.05 by chance alone.
@fig-khan-p-hist shows the p-values:
the spike at the left is the signal,
and the roughly flat remainder looks like p-values from true null hypotheses.
The data alone do not say which of the `r sum(khan_p <= 0.05)` genes are the false positives.

```{r}
#| label: fig-khan-p-hist
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Histogram of the 2308 Welch t-test p-values
#|   comparing tumor classes 2 and 4 in the Khan data.
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Histogram of 2308 p-values in bins of width 0.05.
#|   The first bin, from 0 to 0.05, is far taller than every other bin.
#|   The other bins are much lower:
#|   they decline from the second bin and level off toward a p-value of 1.
ggplot(data.frame(p = khan_p), aes(x = p)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 0.05, boundary = 0, fill = "grey60", color = "white"
  ) +
  labs(x = "p-value", y = "Number of genes")
```
:::
